terms.short: Measures of how an option's price responds to the stock's price (delta, gamma), time (theta) and volatility (vega).

terms.why: Buy one option, sell another nearby: both gain and loss capped.
terms.def: Buying one option and selling another of the same type and expiry at a different strike. It either costs less than the option alone (a debit spread) or pays up front (a credit spread), and caps both the gain and the loss.
terms.short: Buying one option and selling another of the same type and expiry at a different strike.

terms.why: A bet on the size of a move, not its direction.
terms.def: A straddle is a call and a put at the same strike and expiry; a strangle uses a call with a higher strike and a put with a lower one. Buyers win if the price moves far either way; sellers win if it stays quiet.
terms.short: A call and a put of the same expiry, at one strike (straddle) or two (strangle); buyers need big moves.

terms.why: Bets on a range, with the loss capped on both sides.
terms.def: Option combinations that profit if a price ends inside a range. An iron condor sells a put and a call either side of today's price and buys further-out ones as protection, so both the premium collected and the possible loss are capped.
terms.short: Option combinations that profit if the price ends inside a range, with both the possible gain and loss capped.

terms.why: What the books say belongs to the owners.
terms.def: A company's assets minus its liabilities on the balance sheet: the owners' share of the books. It grows with profits kept in the business and with new shares sold, and shrinks with losses, dividends and buybacks.
terms.short: A company's assets minus its liabilities on the balance sheet: the owners' share of the books.

terms.why: The cash the business itself brings in, before investing.
terms.def: The cash a company's day-to-day business generates in a period: net income adjusted for items that use no cash, such as depreciation, and for changes in working capital such as receivables and inventory.
terms.short: The cash a company's day-to-day business generates in a period.

terms.why: The running total of profits kept rather than paid out.
terms.def: The total of a company's profits over its life, less its losses and the dividends it has paid, kept in the business. It sits in shareholders' equity; a negative total is called an accumulated deficit.
terms.short: All the profits a company has kept over its life, after losses and dividends paid; part of shareholders' equity.

terms.why: Spreads the cost of long-lived assets over the years they're used.
terms.def: An expense that spreads the cost of a long-lived asset, such as a machine or a building, over the years it is used; amortization does the same for intangible assets. It lowers reported profit without spending any cash that year.
terms.short: An expense spreading a long-lived asset's cost over its years of use; amortization does the same for intangibles.

terms.why: The committee that sets the Fed's policy rate.
terms.def: The Federal Reserve committee that sets the target range for the federal funds rate and decides on the Fed's bond holdings. It has 12 voting members, meets eight times a year on a published schedule and announces each decision in a statement.
terms.short: The Federal Reserve committee that sets the target range for the federal funds rate, meeting eight times a year.

terms.why: Where Fed officials think the rate should go: a forecast, not a promise.
terms.def: A chart in the Fed's Summary of Economic Projections, published four times a year, showing participants' views of the right federal funds rate at the end of the next few years and in the longer run, without names.
terms.short: A Fed chart, published four times a year, of officials' views on where the federal funds rate should be.

terms.why: A central bank steering interest rates with words, not just decisions.
terms.def: What a central bank says about the likely path of its policy rate. By shaping what markets expect at future meetings, it moves longer-term interest rates without changing today's rate.
terms.short: What a central bank says about the likely path of its policy rate.

terms.why: The size of move S&P 500 options are pricing for the next month.
terms.def: Cboe's index of the volatility S&P 500 options are pricing over the next 30 days, as a yearly percentage. Divide by the square root of 12, about 3.46, for a one-standard-deviation move over a month: a VIX of 20 means roughly ±5.8%.
terms.short: Cboe's index of the volatility S&P 500 options are pricing over the next 30 days, as a yearly percentage.

terms.why: The dollar against six major currencies, mostly the euro.
terms.def: ICE's index of the US dollar against six currencies, weighted 57.6% euro, 13.6% yen, 11.9% pound, 9.1% Canadian dollar, 4.2% Swedish krona and 3.6% Swiss franc. A higher reading means a stronger dollar.
terms.short: ICE's index of the US dollar against six major currencies, mostly the euro; higher means a stronger dollar.

terms.why: The firm on the other side of many trades, hedging rather than betting.
terms.def: A firm that quotes prices to buy and sell all day and earns the gap between them, the bid-ask spread. In options it usually hedges its positions by trading the underlying stock, so its trading can add to or damp price moves.
terms.short: A firm that quotes prices to buy and sell all day and earns the gap between them, the bid-ask spread.

terms.why: How many contracts are still open, not just how many traded.
terms.def: The number of futures or options contracts still open at the end of a day: positions opened and not yet closed or expired. Unlike volume, it doesn't rise when an existing contract simply changes hands.
terms.short: The number of futures or options contracts still open at the end of a day.

terms.why: Options that expire the day they're traded, now most S&P 500 index options volume.
terms.def: Options traded on the day they expire. S&P 500 index options now expire every trading day, and same-day contracts made up 59% of their volume in 2025, by Cboe's count.
terms.short: Options traded on the day they expire; S&P 500 index options now expire every trading day.

terms.why: Says which way a trader wins: from a rise or from a fall.
terms.def: Being long means owning something, or a contract to buy it, so you gain when its price rises. Being short means having sold it, or a contract for it, without owning it, so you gain when the price falls.
terms.example: Buy a futures contract at 100 and sell it at 110: a 10-point gain. Short the same contract and it is a 10-point loss.
terms.short: Long means you gain when the price rises; short means you gain when it falls.

terms.why: The size of the bet, which can dwarf the cash put down.
terms.def: The full value of what a futures or options contract controls: the underlying price times the contract multiplier, a fixed number set by the exchange. A small margin deposit can carry a far larger notional value.
terms.example: One E-mini S&P 500 future is $50 times the index. With the index at 6,000, its notional value is $300,000.
terms.short: The full value a futures or options contract controls: the underlying's price times the contract's fixed multiplier.

terms.why: The official price every futures account is marked to each day.
terms.def: The official price an exchange sets for a futures contract at the end of each day, used to mark every open position to market. At expiry a contract ends either in cash, paid on the final settlement price, or by delivery of the goods.
terms.example: E-mini S&P 500 futures settle in cash; holding a long crude oil contract to the end means taking delivery of 1,000 barrels.
terms.short: The official end-of-day price an exchange sets for a futures contract, used to settle gains and losses.

terms.why: The price for now, which every futures price is measured against.
terms.def: The price for buying something for immediate delivery, as opposed to a futures price for delivery later. As a futures contract nears expiry its price converges on the spot price, because at expiry they are the same thing.
terms.short: The price for buying something now, for immediate delivery, rather than at a later date.

terms.why: Why a commodity in hand can be worth more than one promised later.
terms.def: The benefit of holding a physical commodity rather than a futures contract on it, such as keeping a refinery running when supply is short. When it outweighs storage and interest costs, the spot price rises above later months: backwardation.
terms.short: The extra value of holding a physical commodity now, rather than a contract for it later.

terms.why: Trading away part of a risk you already carry, at a price.
terms.def: Taking a position that gains when an existing exposure loses, to reduce risk. A farmer sells corn futures against a crop; a stockholder buys a put. A hedge gives up some upside, or costs a premium, in exchange for a narrower range of outcomes.
terms.short: Taking an offsetting position to reduce a risk you already carry, at the cost of some upside or a premium.

terms.why: The trading that keeps related prices from drifting apart.
terms.def: Buying something where it is cheap and selling the same thing, or its equivalent, where it is dear, locking in a profit with little or no risk. Arbitrageurs' trading pushes the two prices back together, which is why futures track fair value.
terms.short: Buying something cheap and selling its equivalent dear at the same time, locking in a near-riskless profit.

terms.why: The private handshake that futures contracts standardized.
terms.def: A private agreement to buy or sell something on a future date at a price fixed today. Unlike a futures contract, it is negotiated privately, not exchange-traded, and usually settles once, at the end, so each side relies on the other to pay.
terms.short: A private deal to buy or sell later at a price fixed today, settled once at the end.

terms.why: The two oil prices the news quotes, and they are not the same oil.
terms.def: The two benchmark crude oil prices. WTI (West Texas Intermediate) is US light crude, delivered at Cushing, Oklahoma, under NYMEX futures contracts. Brent, the international benchmark, is named for a North Sea oil field and trades on ICE.
terms.short: The two benchmark crude oil prices: WTI for US crude, delivered in Oklahoma, and Brent internationally.

terms.why: The two words traders use to read every central bank remark.
terms.def: Hawkish means leaning toward higher interest rates to fight inflation; dovish means leaning toward lower rates to support jobs and growth. Traders apply the words to central bankers, statements and decisions, and markets move on how hawkish or dovish they are against what was expected.
terms.short: Hawkish leans toward higher rates to fight inflation; dovish toward lower rates to support jobs and growth.

terms.term: Quantitative easing and tightening (QE and QT)
terms.why: How a central bank moves long-term rates without touching its policy rate.
terms.def: Quantitative easing is a central bank buying bonds, such as Treasuries and mortgage bonds, to push long-term interest rates down. Quantitative tightening is the reverse: letting those bonds mature without replacing them, or selling them. Tapering means slowing the purchases.
terms.short: A central bank buying bonds to push long-term rates down (QE), or shrinking those holdings (QT).

terms.why: Where the market's odds for each Fed meeting come from.
terms.def: Futures that settle on a month's average effective federal funds rate, quoted as 100 minus that rate. Comparing a month's price with today's rate shows what traders expect the Fed to do at a meeting, the source of the odds quoted in the news.
terms.example: A price of 96.00 means traders expect the rate to average 4.00% over that month.
terms.short: Futures on a month's average federal funds rate; their prices imply the odds traders give each Fed decision.

terms.why: The inflation numbers that move rates, bonds and the Fed.
terms.def: The two main US inflation gauges. The Consumer Price Index (Bureau of Labor Statistics) tracks prices urban consumers pay. The broader PCE price index (Bureau of Economic Analysis) is the measure behind the Fed's 2% goal. Core versions leave out food and energy.
terms.short: The main US inflation gauges: the Consumer Price Index and the PCE price index, the Fed's chosen measure.

terms.why: Market shorthand for whether money is chasing gains or running for cover.
terms.def: Shorthand for the market's mood. On risk-on days money buys stocks, high-yield bonds and growth-sensitive currencies; on risk-off days it moves toward assets seen as safe, such as Treasuries, the US dollar, the yen and gold. It is a tendency, not a rule.
terms.short: Shorthand for the market's mood: buying riskier assets (risk-on) or running to safer ones (risk-off).

terms.why: A right you pay for, not an obligation: the core of every options trade.
terms.def: A contract giving its buyer the right, not the obligation, to buy (a call) or sell (a put) something at a set price, the strike, until or on a set date, the expiry. The buyer pays the seller, or writer, a premium.
terms.example: Listed US stock options cover 100 shares each, so a premium quoted at $5 costs $500 a contract.
terms.short: A contract giving the right, not the obligation, to buy or sell at a set price by a set date.

terms.why: When an option is actually used, and who has to deliver.
terms.def: Exercising is an option buyer using the right to buy or sell at the strike; the seller chosen to fulfill it is assigned. American-style options, like US stock options, can be exercised any day to expiry; European-style, like S&P 500 index options, only at expiry.
terms.short: Using an option's right to buy or sell at the strike; the seller picked to fulfill it is assigned.

terms.why: Splits an option's price into what it's worth now and what time adds.
terms.def: An option's premium has two parts. Intrinsic value is what exercising today would pay, zero if out of the money. Time value is the rest: the price of the chance it gains before expiry. It shrinks as expiry nears, faster at the end: time decay.
terms.example: A $90-strike call on a $100 stock priced at $12 holds $10 of intrinsic value and $2 of time value.
terms.short: An option's price splits into intrinsic value, what exercising now would pay, and time value, the rest.

terms.why: The standard formula for an option's fair price, and the source of implied volatility.
terms.def: The 1973 formula, from Fischer Black, Myron Scholes and Robert Merton, for the fair price of a European option from five inputs: the stock price, strike, time to expiry, interest rate and volatility. Traders run it backward to turn market prices into implied volatility.
terms.short: The standard formula for an option's fair price, from the stock price, strike, time, interest rate and volatility.

terms.why: Ties call and put prices together, so neither can drift far from the other.
terms.def: The fixed link between the prices of a call and a put on the same stock, strike and expiry: for European options on a stock without dividends, call minus put equals the stock price minus the strike's present value. Arbitrage keeps it holding.
terms.example: Stock $100, strike $100, 90 days at 4%: the call costs about $0.98 more than the put.
terms.short: The fixed price link between a call and a put on the same stock, strike and expiry.

terms.why: Income now, in exchange for giving up gains above the strike.
terms.def: Owning a stock and selling a call option on it. The premium is income now, but any gain above the strike goes to the call's buyer, while the downside stays with the owner. Some ETFs run the strategy across an index to pay higher distributions.
terms.example: Own a $100 stock and sell the $110 call for about $2: you keep the $2, but your gains stop at $110.
terms.short: Owning a stock and selling a call on it: premium income now, in exchange for capped gains.

terms.why: Insurance for a stock you own, with the premium as the cost.
terms.def: Owning a stock and buying a put option on it. The put sets a floor: below the strike, its gain offsets the stock's loss. The premium is the cost of that insurance, paid whether or not the stock falls.
terms.example: Own a $100 stock and buy the $90 put for about $1: by expiry the most you can lose is about $11 a share.
terms.short: Owning a stock and buying a put on it, which caps the loss below the strike for a premium.

terms.why: A daily gauge of options traders' mood, read as fear or greed.
terms.def: Put volume divided by call volume over a day; Cboe publishes several, for stocks, indexes and S&P 500 options. A high ratio is read as fear and a low one as greed.
terms.short: Put options traded divided by call options traded, read as a gauge of fear or greed.

terms.why: Whether option dealers' hedging calms the market or feeds its moves.
terms.def: Option dealers hedge by trading the stock. Short options, they are short gamma: they buy as prices rise and sell as they fall, feeding moves. Long options, they are long gamma, and their hedging damps moves. Published gamma exposure (GEX) figures are estimates.
terms.short: Whether option dealers' hedging chases price moves (short gamma) or leans against them (long gamma).

terms.why: How heavy call buying can force dealers to chase a rising stock.
terms.def: A loop in which heavy buying of call options leads the dealers who sold them to buy the stock to hedge; the rising price raises the calls' delta, prompting more buying.
terms.short: A loop where dealers who sold calls buy the stock to hedge, pushing it higher and prompting more buying.

terms.why: The days when large batches of options and futures expire at once.
terms.def: Monthly US stock and index options expire on the third Friday of the month. In March, June, September and December, stock index futures expire that day too: triple witching, for the three kinds of contract. Trading volume often jumps.
terms.short: Monthly options expire on the third Friday; in March, June, September and December, index futures expire too: triple witching.

terms.why: The baseline return every riskier investment has to beat.
terms.def: The return on an investment with no default risk over its life, usually taken as the yield on short-term government bills such as US Treasury bills. It anchors option pricing, the Sharpe ratio and the return investors demand from stocks. It still carries inflation risk.
terms.short: The return on a default-free investment, usually short-term government bills: the baseline other investments must beat.

terms.why: A loan you can buy and sell: fixed payments, then your money back.
terms.def: A loan to a government or company that pays fixed interest, the coupon, usually twice a year, and repays its face value on a set date, the maturity. Bonds trade after issue, so prices move as interest rates and the borrower's credit change.
terms.short: A loan to a government or company that usually pays fixed interest and repays its face value at maturity.

terms.why: The amount a bond repays, and the base its coupon is figured on.
terms.def: The amount a bond or bill repays at maturity, usually $1,000 a bond, and the amount its coupon rate is applied to. A bond priced above it trades at a premium, below it at a discount. Preferred shares have a par value too, often $25.
terms.short: The amount a bond repays at maturity, and the base its coupon rate is applied to.

terms.why: When the loan ends, and a big part of how far its price can swing.
terms.def: The date a bond's face value is repaid and the bond ends, or the time left until then. Longer maturities usually pay higher yields and swing more when rates change. Treasury bills run up to a year, notes 2 to 10, bonds 20 or 30.
terms.short: The date a bond repays its face value and ends, or the time left until then.

terms.why: The extra yield lenders demand for the risk of not being repaid.
terms.def: The extra yield a bond pays over a government bond of the same maturity: the market's price for the chance the borrower won't repay in full. Spreads widen when investors grow nervous about defaults and narrow when they relax.
terms.example: A 10-year company bond yielding 6% when the 10-year Treasury yields 4% has a credit spread of 2 points, or 200 basis points.
terms.short: The extra yield a bond pays over a government bond of the same maturity, for the risk of default.

terms.why: The chance a borrower doesn't pay, which every bond's yield prices in.
terms.def: The chance a borrower fails to pay interest or repay principal on time. Failing to is a default, and lenders then often recover only part of what they lent. Ratings and credit spreads measure it. A skipped preferred dividend is not a default.
terms.short: The chance a borrower fails to pay interest or repay on time; failing to pay is a default.

terms.why: Bonds from US states and cities, often free of federal income tax.
terms.def: A bond issued by a US state, city or other local government or agency, often to pay for schools, roads or utilities. Interest on most is free of federal income tax, so their yields are compared with taxable bonds on an after-tax basis.
terms.short: A bond issued by a US state, city or local agency, with interest usually free of federal income tax.

terms.term: Real return and real interest rate
terms.why: What your money actually gains once inflation is taken out.
terms.def: A return or interest rate after inflation: roughly the stated, or nominal, rate minus the inflation rate. It measures the change in what your money can buy. Exactly, it is (1 + nominal rate) ÷ (1 + inflation rate) − 1.
terms.example: Cash earning 4% a year while prices rise 3% has a real return of about 1%.
terms.short: A return or interest rate after inflation: roughly the stated rate minus the inflation rate.

terms.why: What protects a bank deposit if the bank fails, and up to how much.
terms.def: Government protection for deposits if a bank fails. In the US the FDIC covers up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category; in Canada CDIC covers up to C$100,000 per category, per member institution. Money market funds and crypto are not covered.
terms.short: Government protection for bank deposits if a bank fails, up to $250,000 per depositor, bank and category in the US.

terms.why: A pooled fund you buy from and sell back to, priced once a day.
terms.def: A pooled fund that issues units, or shares, to investors and invests the money under a manager's stated rules. You buy from and sell back to the fund itself, at its net asset value set once a day after the close, not on an exchange.
terms.short: A pooled fund you buy from and sell back to directly, at a price set once a day.

terms.why: Whether a manager picks investments, and whether the fee buys an edge.
terms.def: An actively managed fund's manager picks investments to try to beat a benchmark index; a passive fund copies the index. Active funds usually charge more, and over long periods most have trailed their benchmarks after fees.
terms.short: Active funds pick investments to try to beat a benchmark; passive funds copy the index.

terms.why: Built for one day's move; held longer, results can drift far from it.
terms.def: Funds that aim for a multiple of an index's daily return, such as two or three times, or its opposite. They reset daily, so over months results can drift far from that multiple, and choppy markets can erode them even when the index ends flat.
terms.example: An index falls 10% one day and rises 11.1% the next, ending flat. A 3x fund loses 30%, then gains 33.3%: down about 7%.
terms.short: Funds that aim for a multiple, or the opposite, of an index's daily move, reset every day.

terms.why: Trades like an ETF, but it is an IOU from a bank.
terms.def: A bank's unsecured debt that trades on an exchange and pays out according to an index, minus fees. Unlike an ETF it holds no basket for its owners: if the issuing bank fails, holders are its creditors. Some can be redeemed early by the issuer.
terms.short: A bank's debt that trades like an ETF and pays according to an index, without holding a basket.

terms.why: The document that says what a security or fund is, costs and risks.
terms.def: The legal document an issuer must give investors when offering securities, setting out the terms, fees, risks and how the money will be used. Funds publish one too; in Canada a short Fund Facts or ETF Facts sheet summarizes it.
terms.short: The legal document that sets out a security's or fund's terms, fees and risks for investors.

terms.why: Spreading money across many holdings so no single failure sinks you.
terms.def: Spreading money across many investments so the failure of any one does limited harm. It cuts the risk of single companies, not of the whole market falling. Concentration is the opposite: a few holdings, or index giants, driving most of the result.
terms.short: Spreading money across many investments so no single one can do much harm; concentration is the opposite.

terms.why: The profit on a sale, and the gain or loss that exists only on paper.
terms.def: The rise in an investment's value above what was paid for it. It is unrealized, a gain or loss on paper, until the investment is sold; then it is realized and, in a taxable account, usually taxed. Funds pass realized gains to holders as distributions.
terms.short: The profit from an investment's rise in value: unrealized on paper until sold, realized when sold.

terms.why: Whoever holds the keys holds the coins.
terms.def: Owning crypto means controlling a private key, a secret code that authorizes moves on the blockchain. A wallet, software or a device, stores the keys. Self-custody means holding them yourself; on an exchange, it holds them. Lost with no backup, a key can't be recovered.
terms.short: A private key is the secret code that moves crypto on a blockchain; a wallet stores the keys.

terms.why: The company's score for a period, from sales down to profit.
terms.def: The financial statement that shows a company's revenue, costs and profit over a period, a quarter or a year: from sales at the top, through gross profit and operating income, to net income at the bottom.
terms.short: The financial statement showing a company's revenue, costs and profit over a quarter or a year.

terms.why: A snapshot of what a company owns and owes on one date.
terms.def: The financial statement that lists what a company owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities) and the owners' stake (equity) on one date. It always balances: assets equal liabilities plus equity.
terms.short: A snapshot of what a company owns, what it owes and the owners' stake on one date.

terms.why: Follows the actual cash, which profit alone can hide.
terms.def: The financial statement that shows the cash a company took in and paid out over a period, in three sections: operating activities (running the business), investing activities (equipment, acquisitions, securities) and financing activities (borrowing, repaying, issuing shares, dividends and buybacks).
terms.short: The financial statement tracking cash in and out over a period: operating, investing and financing activities.

terms.why: The bottom line: what is left for the owners after every cost.
terms.def: A company's profit for a period after all costs, interest and taxes: the bottom line of the income statement. Divided by the share count it gives earnings per share; whatever isn't paid out as dividends is added to retained earnings.
terms.short: A company's profit after every cost, interest payment and tax: the bottom line of the income statement.

terms.term: Cost of goods sold (cost of sales)
terms.why: The direct cost of what was sold, the first cut out of revenue.
terms.def: The direct cost of the goods or services a company sold in a period, such as materials, parts and factory labor. Revenue minus it is gross profit; overheads such as marketing and research sit below it, in operating expenses.
terms.short: The direct cost of what a company sold; revenue minus it is gross profit.

terms.why: The cost of running the business, beyond the direct cost of what it sells.
terms.def: The costs of running a business beyond the direct cost of what it sells: wages, rent, marketing, administration and, at many companies, research and development. Gross profit minus operating expenses is operating income.
terms.short: The costs of running a business beyond the direct cost of what it sells: wages, rent, marketing, research and administration.

terms.why: The cash tied up in running the business day to day.
terms.def: Current assets minus current liabilities. Current assets turn into cash within a year (cash, receivables, inventory); current liabilities fall due within one (payables, short-term debt). A rise in working capital ties up cash, which is why operating cash flow subtracts it.
terms.short: Current assets minus current liabilities: the money tied up in running the business day to day.

terms.why: Sales already counted as revenue but not yet collected in cash.
terms.def: Money customers owe a company for goods or services already delivered and counted as revenue. It sits in current assets. A rise uses cash, and receivables growing faster than sales can mean the company is struggling to collect.
terms.short: Money customers owe for sales already made and counted as revenue, but not yet paid.

terms.why: Bills a company owes its suppliers: cash it has kept, for now.
terms.def: Money a company owes its suppliers for goods and services already received. It sits in current liabilities. A rise means the company has kept cash for now, which lifts operating cash flow until the bills are paid.
terms.short: Money a company owes suppliers for goods or services it has already received.

terms.why: Why profit and cash differ, and why both statements matter.
terms.def: Recording revenue when it is earned and costs when they are incurred, whatever the timing of the cash. A sale on credit counts as revenue now; an oven's cost is spread over its life as depreciation. Public companies report this way.
terms.short: Recording revenue when earned and costs when incurred, rather than when cash changes hands.

terms.why: A dollar later is worth less than a dollar now; this says how much less.
terms.def: What money due in the future is worth today. Discounting divides each future amount by (1 + rate) once for every year of waiting, so higher rates and longer waits shrink it more. Valuing an asset from its future cash this way is a DCF.
terms.example: At 5% a year, $100 due in ten years is worth about $61 today; at 3%, about $74.
terms.short: What money due in the future is worth today, shrunk by an interest rate for each year of waiting.

terms.why: Shows why small changes in growth or rates swing a stock's value.
terms.def: A way to value a stock whose dividend grows at a steady rate forever: next year's dividend divided by the required return minus the growth rate. It works only when the required return exceeds growth, and small changes in either move the value a lot.
terms.example: Next year's $2 dividend, growing 5% a year after, with an 8% required return: $2 ÷ (0.08 − 0.05) ≈ $66.67.
terms.short: Values a stock as next year's dividend divided by the required return minus the dividend's growth rate.

terms.why: The return investors demand, which sets what they'll pay today.
terms.def: The yearly return investors demand for an investment's risk: roughly a safe government bond's yield plus a risk premium. For the stock market, that extra is the equity risk premium. Future cash is discounted at this rate, so when it rises, prices fall.
terms.short: The yearly return investors demand for an investment's risk: a safe bond's yield plus a risk premium.

terms.why: P/E flipped over, so a stock can be set beside a bond's yield.
terms.def: A company's earnings per share divided by its share price: the P/E ratio turned upside down. It shows profit per dollar of stock, which can be set beside a bond's yield, though a company's earnings can grow and a bond's coupon can't.
terms.example: A P/E of 25 is an earnings yield of 1 ÷ 25 = 4%.
terms.short: Earnings per share divided by the share price: the P/E ratio turned upside down, as a percentage.

terms.why: Two styles of stock that react differently to rates and the economy.
terms.def: Growth stocks are priced for fast future growth, usually at high P/E ratios, with most of their profits expected years out. Value stocks trade at low prices relative to earnings or book value, often in mature businesses. Rising rates tend to hit growth stocks harder.
terms.short: Growth stocks are priced for fast future growth; value stocks trade cheaply against today's earnings or assets.

terms.why: A share sale that gives existing owners first claim, usually at a discount.
terms.def: A sale of new shares offered first to existing shareholders, in proportion to what they already hold, usually at a discount to the market price. Where the rights can be traded, an owner who doesn't want the new shares can sell the rights instead.
terms.short: A sale of new shares offered first to existing owners, in proportion to their holdings, usually at a discount.

terms.why: Debt that can turn into shares: dilution waiting to happen.
terms.def: A bond the holder can exchange for a set number of the company's shares, usually paying a lower coupon than a plain bond in return. Converted, it becomes new shares, which is why the diluted share count counts them in advance when they would dilute.
terms.short: A bond the holder can swap for a set number of the company's shares, usually paying a lower coupon.

terms.why: A property's own profit before loans: the number cap rates are built on.
terms.def: A property's rental and other income minus the costs of running it, such as maintenance, property taxes and insurance, before loan interest, income taxes and depreciation. Divided by the property's value, it gives the cap rate.
terms.example: A building earning $1 million a year of NOI, valued at a 5% cap rate, is worth $20 million.
terms.short: A property's income minus its running costs, before loan interest, income taxes and depreciation.

terms.why: How much an option moves with the stock, and so how big a hedge is.
terms.def: How much an option's price changes for a $1 move in the stock: 0 to 1 for calls, 0 to −1 for puts. At the money it is about 0.5 (−0.5 for a put). Dealers buy or sell delta's worth of shares to hedge.
terms.example: A call with a delta of 0.5 gains about $0.50 when the stock rises $1; 100 contracts of 100 shares each move like 5,000 shares.
terms.short: Change in an option's price per $1 stock move: 0 to 1 for calls, 0 to −1 for puts.

terms.why: Says how fast an option's risk changes, and how hard hedgers must trade.
terms.def: How much an option's delta changes for a $1 move in the stock. It is largest for at-the-money options near expiry, where a small move swings delta most. Option buyers are long gamma; sellers are short gamma.
terms.example: A call with delta 0.50 and gamma 0.05: after a $1 rise in the stock, its delta is about 0.55.
terms.short: How much an option's delta changes for a $1 move in the stock; largest near the strike close to expiry.

terms.why: The daily cost of holding an option, or the daily income of selling one.
terms.def: How much an option's price falls each day as expiry nears, all else unchanged: time decay. It speeds up in the final weeks, most for at-the-money options. Buyers pay it; sellers collect it.
terms.example: An option worth $3.00 with a theta of −0.05 would be worth about $2.95 tomorrow if nothing else changed.
terms.short: How much an option loses in value each day as expiry nears, all else unchanged: time decay.

terms.why: Shows how much an option's price rides on expected volatility.
terms.def: How much an option's price changes when implied volatility moves one percentage point. Longer-dated and at-the-money options have the most. Buyers gain when implied volatility rises, sellers when it falls.
terms.example: An option with a vega of 0.20 gains about $0.20 if implied volatility rises from 25% to 26%.
terms.short: How much an option's price changes when implied volatility moves by one percentage point.

terms.term: In, at and out of the money
terms.why: Says whether an option would be worth anything if exercised today.
terms.def: Where the stock stands against an option's strike. A call is in the money when the stock is above the strike, a put when it is below; at the money when the two are about equal; otherwise out of the money, with no intrinsic value.
terms.example: Stock at $105: the $100 call is $5 in the money; the $110 call and the $100 put are out of the money.
terms.short: Whether exercising an option today would pay: in the money it would; at or out of the money it wouldn't.

terms.why: The contract usually quoted as 'the price' of oil or a stock index.
terms.def: The futures contract closest to expiry, usually the most traded, and the one news reports quote as the price. As it nears expiry, traders roll into the next month, which then becomes the front month.
terms.example: In early April the May US crude (WTI) contract is the front month; once it expires around April 20, June takes its place.
terms.short: The futures contract closest to expiry, usually the most traded and the one quoted as 'the price'.

terms.why: Why a stock sometimes sticks near a big strike on expiry day.
terms.def: A stock closing at or near a strike with large open interest on expiration day. Dealers' hedging around the strike can help hold it there. Studies find the effect in some stocks; it is far from reliable.
terms.short: A stock closing near a strike with large open interest on expiry day, partly from dealers' hedging.

terms.why: The first profit line: what selling earns before running the business.
terms.def: Revenue minus the cost of goods sold: what is left from sales after the direct cost of making or buying what was sold, before marketing, research, administration and other running costs. Divided by revenue, it is the gross margin.
terms.example: A shop sells $100,000 of goods that cost it $60,000: gross profit is $40,000, a 40% gross margin.
terms.short: Revenue minus the direct cost of what was sold, before the costs of running the business.

terms.why: Profit from the business itself, before interest and taxes.
terms.def: Gross profit minus operating expenses such as wages, rent, marketing and research: what the business earns from its operations before interest and taxes. Divided by revenue, it is the operating margin.
terms.example: $40,000 of gross profit less $25,000 of running costs leaves $15,000 of operating income.
terms.short: What a business earns from its operations: gross profit minus running costs, before interest and taxes.

terms.why: Goods waiting to be sold: cash tied up until customers buy.
terms.def: Goods a company holds to sell, and the materials to make them, carried on the balance sheet at cost, or less if their value falls. Buying inventory uses cash before any sale; when the goods sell, their cost moves to cost of goods sold.
terms.example: A pizza shop's flour and cheese are inventory until the pizzas sell; then their cost becomes cost of goods sold.
terms.short: Goods a company holds to sell, and materials to make them, carried at cost or lower on the balance sheet.

terms.why: Separates what lasts, or falls due, beyond a year from the near term.
terms.def: On a balance sheet, assets expected to serve the company for more than a year, such as buildings, equipment and patents, and debts due after more than a year, such as long-term loans and bonds. Current items are those within a year.
terms.short: Assets kept for more than a year, like equipment, and debts due after more than a year, like bonds.

terms.why: Why a shareholder can lose what they paid, but never more.
terms.def: The rule that a company's shareholders are not personally responsible for its debts. If the company fails, owners can lose what they paid for their shares, but creditors cannot come after their other money.
terms.example: Buy $1,000 of shares in a company that goes bankrupt owing billions: you lose the $1,000 and owe nothing more.
terms.short: Shareholders aren't liable for a company's debts: the most they can lose is what they paid for their shares.

terms.why: The trader who takes on the risk a hedger wants to shed.
terms.def: A trader who takes on price risk to profit from expected moves, with no business need for the underlying. In futures, speculators often take the other side of hedgers' trades, which makes it easier to buy and sell.
terms.short: A trader who takes on price risk to profit from expected moves, often the other side of a hedger.

terms.why: A fund that quietly stops doing what you bought it for.
terms.def: When a fund's holdings move away from its stated style or mandate, such as a value fund buying growth stocks, or a small-cap fund keeping companies that have grown large. Investors end up with exposure they didn't choose.
terms.short: When a fund's holdings move away from its stated style, such as a value fund buying growth stocks.
